newsitem.title: GERMANY: German firms could pay tax on shift work - BDI.
newsitem.headline: German firms could pay tax on shift work - BDI.

text.p: Germany's industry lobby joined the national tax debate on Monday by offering a way out of a stalemate over scrapping tax relief on pay for unsocial work hours, but attacked plans to back-tax extraordinary earnings.

The Federation of German Industry (BDI) confirmed reports its head Hans-Olaf Henkel had met Finance Minister Theo Waigel last week to float the idea of companies paying 10 percent tax on wages for night, Sunday and holiday work.
Waigel's plans to cut 30 billion marks in taxes envisage abolishing the tax relief on unusual work hours -- but that is strongly opposed by the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) and trade unions.
BDI spokesman Dieter Rath told Reuters his organisation's proposal would prevent new social insurance costs -- which already total over 40 percent of wages -- from arising.
If the tax relief is scrapped, "we would also have to fear...that trade unions would seek higher compensation at the next pay round," Rath said.
Rath said that the extra sum brought into federal coffers through the 10 percent tax payment would be "not insignificant" but did not put a figure on the amount.
No comment was immediately available from the Finance Ministry.
The BDI, however, strongly opposes government plans to impose planned lower corporate tax rates on extraordinary earnings retroactively from the start of 1997.
The earliest such a decision could come would be when the measure is approved by Chancellor Helmut Kohl's cabinet, Rath confirmed.

The coalition and SPD will hold a third round of cross-party tax reform talks this Saturday to try to reach an early deal to cut taxes and encourage investment as Germany tries to boost its economy in the runup to European monetary union (EMU).
